home.title: SignAI — AI Sign Language Translation in Real Time
home.description: SignAI builds AI that recognizes sign language from an ordinary camera and turns it into text. Starting with German Sign Language (DGS).
home.og_title: SignAI — Sign language, understood in real time
home.h1: Sign language to text, in real time.
home.lead: SignAI watches sign language through an ordinary camera and writes out what was signed. We’re starting with German Sign Language and building toward products for the everyday conversations where no interpreter is around.

why.photo_alt: Two friends talking in sign language over lunch in a café.
why.title: Communication shouldn’t depend on who is available to interpret.
why.lead: Sign languages are full languages, with their own grammar, vocabulary and dialects. But a meeting at work, a lecture, a quick question at a counter: most of daily life runs on spoken language. Interpreters are essential. There just aren’t enough of them to be at every one of those moments.

Deaf people in Germany. For many of them, DGS is their first language.

mission.photo_alt: Two people sign to each other on a winter street, hands in focus.
mission.title: Conversations that don’t wait for an interpreter.
mission.text: Today, many conversations between Deaf and hearing people run on handwritten notes or waiting for an interpreter. We’re building products that let everyone use their own language, with just a camera in between.

points.title: In your own language
points.text: Sign the way you normally would. SignAI handles the text.

points.title: In real time
points.text: Nothing to book, nothing to wait for. The text appears while you sign.

points.title: With what you have
points.text: No gloves, sensors or special hardware. A regular camera is enough.

how.photo_alt: A man signs on a video call while the person he is talking to signs into the laptop camera.
how.title: From camera to conversation.

steps.title: Capture
steps.text: A standard webcam or phone camera. That’s the whole setup.

steps.title: Understand
steps.text: SignAI tracks the hands, body, face and mouth. In sign language, all four carry meaning.

steps.title: Translate
steps.text: A sequence model turns what it sees into glosses, and glosses into readable sentences.

steps.title: Read
steps.text: The translation shows up as plain text, right as it’s signed.

tech.title: Built on how sign language actually works.
tech.text: The hands are only part of it. Facial expressions mark questions, mouth patterns tell otherwise identical signs apart, and movement through space carries grammar. Our next-generation model reads all of it at once.

streams.title: Body & movement
streams.text: Pose keypoints over time capture location, motion and rhythm.

streams.title: Hands
streams.text: A vision transformer reads hand shape and orientation for both hands.

streams.title: Face & mouth
streams.text: Mouthings and facial grammar resolve meaning the hands alone cannot.

streams.title: Fusion
streams.text: All three streams combine into one representation of what was signed.

items.title: Sign language first
items.text: DGS is a full language with its own grammar. We don’t treat it as a set of gestures to decode.

items.title: Complementing interpreters
items.text: SignAI is for everyday moments. At the doctor’s, in court, or anywhere else a mistake is costly, you want a professional interpreter.

items.title: Privacy by design
items.text: We process video to translate it, not to keep it. As much as possible should run on your own device.

items.title: Honest about accuracy
items.text: We test on clips the model never trains on, publish results only once the evaluation is done, and are open about what it cannot do yet.

items.title: Shaped with the community
items.text: We want Deaf signers, interpreters and researchers to test what we build and tell us where it’s wrong.

items.title: Open research
items.text: Our research code is public, so methods can be inspected, reproduced and improved.

items.a: SignAI is an AI system that recognizes sign language from ordinary video and translates it into text in real time. For now it works with German Sign Language (DGS, Deutsche Gebärdensprache). We’re turning it into products for everyday conversations between Deaf and hearing people.
We’re training the next model now and getting the first products ready. Sign up for updates and we’ll email you on launch day.

items.q: Where can I download the SignAI desktop app?
items.a: The first-generation desktop prototype for Windows has been retired, and downloads are paused while we build the next SignAI. Read more.

items.q: Which sign languages does SignAI support?
items.a: SignAI is trained on German Sign Language (DGS). Additional sign languages, starting with American Sign Language (ASL), are on our roadmap.

items.q: Will SignAI replace sign language interpreters?
items.a: No. For medical appointments, legal matters and anything else where a mistake is costly, you need a professional interpreter. SignAI is for the moments when no interpreter is there, which is most of them.

Our current sentence model covers a vocabulary of more than 800 DGS glosses and translates short sentences of up to around 15 signs. It works best with clear signing and good lighting. The next-generation model is tested on a held-out set of clips it never trains on, and we will publish results once evaluation is complete.

We collect as little as we can. Video is processed to produce a translation and isn’t stored by default. Where possible, we want recognition to run on your own device. Your data is never used for research without your explicit consent.
Our research code is publicly available on GitHub under a non-commercial license. For commercial use, licensing or partnerships, please contact us.

items.q: How can I work with SignAI?
items.a: We are looking for research collaborators for datasets, evaluation and compute, organizations that care about accessibility, and members of the Deaf community who want to help shape what we build. Write to hello@signai.dev.

technology.title: SignAI Technology — How AI Recognizes Sign Language
technology.description: How SignAI recognizes sign language: body, hand and mouth streams fused into one model, trained on the Public DGS Corpus and read sign by sign into sentences.
technology.lead: Sign language uses the hands, the face, the body and the space around the signer, all at once. SignAI reads them together: three streams, fused into one model.
hero_meta: Trained on the Public DGS Corpus

pipeline.title: From pixels to sentences.
pipeline.lead: Five stages, from raw video to text you can read.
pipeline.photo_alt: A woman in a café signs on a video call on her tablet.

steps.title: Video
steps.text: Standard RGB video from a webcam or phone.

steps.title: Landmarks & crops
steps.text: 49 body and hand landmarks per frame, plus crops of both hands and the mouth.

steps.title: Three streams
steps.text: Movement, hand shape and mouth patterns, each with its own encoder.

steps.title: Sign
steps.text: The fused features are classified as one sign, written as a gloss.

steps.title: Sentence
steps.text: Sign by sign, the glosses become a readable sentence.

model.title: Three streams, fused into one.
model.lead: Many signs share the same hand movement and differ only in hand shape, facial expression or mouthing. So our model gives each channel its own encoder, then fuses the three.

streams.title: Body & movement
streams.text: Seven upper-body points and 21 points per hand become per-landmark heatmaps over 32 frames. A 3D convolutional network (SlowOnly ResNet-50) reads location, movement and rhythm from them.

streams.title: Hands
streams.text: Crops of both hands go through a frozen DINOv3 vision transformer. A small temporal transformer, shared by both hands, follows hand shape and orientation over time.

streams.title: Face & mouth
streams.text: Mouth crops pass through the same design to capture mouthings and facial expression. Without them, signs with identical hand movements look the same.

model.fusion: The three features are joined into one 1,536-dimensional vector and classified together. DINOv3 runs once, offline, so training only touches cached features and stays fast and reproducible.

translation.title: From single signs to sentences.
translation.p1: The word model is the foundation. It recognizes one sign at a time and names it as a gloss, the written label linguists use for a sign.
translation.p2: For sentences, the same model reads a signed sentence sign by sign. The result is a sequence of glosses, like MORGEN REGEN NORD.
translation.p3: Glosses follow the grammar of sign language, not of German. A separate language step, which we’re building next, turns them into fluent sentences.
translation.code_output: Tomorrow it will rain in the north.
translation.code_aria: Simplified architecture of the word model

data.title: Learned from real conversations.
data.lead: SignAI doesn’t learn from staged word lists. It learns from Deaf people signing naturally, cut into single signs. We’ll publish accuracy once the evaluation is done.

cards.title: Natural signing data
cards.text: We train on the Public DGS Corpus: conversations between Deaf signers from all over Germany. Its expert annotations mark where each sign starts and ends, so every sign becomes its own clip.

cards.title: Camera-proof preprocessing
cards.text: Keypoints are centered on the shoulders, scaled by shoulder width, interpolated where landmarks drop out and smoothed over time. Every clip is resampled to 32 frames.

cards.title: Fair across skin tones and rooms
cards.text: Hand and mouth crops are color-corrected (Shades of Gray), so lighting and skin tone matter less. Augmentation for skin tone, color, framing and blur is in the works.

cards.title: A clean test set
cards.text: Signs with fewer than five examples are left out. The rest are split per sign into training, validation and test sets, and the model never trains on the test set.

items.title: Fingerspelling
items.text: A dedicated classifier for the manual alphabet handles names, places and terms without an established sign.

items.title: Thousands of signs
items.text: Scaling the vocabulary from hundreds to thousands of glosses with larger datasets and more compute.

items.title: Continuous signing
items.text: Finding where one sign ends and the next begins, so the word model can read whole sentences on its own.

items.title: Fluent output
items.text: Turning gloss sequences into natural, grammatical written language.

items.title: More sign languages
items.text: Extending beyond DGS, starting with American Sign Language (ASL).

items.title: On-device inference
items.text: Efficient models that run locally for lower latency and stronger privacy.

open.title: Research in the open.
open.text: Our research code is public. If you work on sign language, computer vision or accessibility, get in touch.
